facts.claim: Wright argues natural selection designed the human mind to crave: it favors traits that do a good job of getting genes into the next generation, not traits that make people content. Never-ending dissatisfaction helped ancestors reproduce.
The happiness of reaching a goal tends to fade; evolutionary psychology's explanation is that, without fading, animals would stop pursuing food and sex.
Wright's hiking example: every rustle in the underbrush produces a surge of fear. The fear can be adaptive even if no snake is there, since selection favors a false alarm ('better safe than sorry').

Public speaking induces anxiety in many people, even sleeplessness before a presentation. Wright says we are not designed for that situation: ancestral life had no large public talks, so an old response fires in a new setting.

Wright says mindfulness meditation can quiet the mind enough to begin freeing you from some mechanisms of distortion; if you change how you relate to anxiety and stop identifying with it, that is an incremental realisation of not-self. Observing feelings without acting on them is not suppression.
On a retreat Wright felt 'the bounds of myself had dissolved'; a bird singing outside the meditation hall seemed 'no less a part of me than a tingling in my foot'.
Wright's version of Buddhism is secular, centred on mindfulness meditation, without supernatural beliefs; critics question both his naturalised Buddhism and his evolutionary psychology.
